title: Forces and Pressure
seo_title: Secondary 2 Science: Forces and Pressure Worksheets (Lower Secondary Science with Answers)
standard_code: Secondary 2: Application of Forces and Transfer of Energy (Forces and pressure)
standard_text: Distinguish contact forces such as friction from non-contact forces such as magnetic and gravitational forces; recognise that a force can change an object's motion, cause a turning effect, change its size or shape, or exert pressure; measure force in newtons and compare weight and mass; investigate pressure using pressure = force / area and appreciate examples such as high heels, knives, suction cups, straws and submarines (summary of the MOE Lower Secondary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 2 science worksheets for Singapore students on forces and pressure: contact and non-contact forces, effects of forces, mass and weight, pressure = force / area. With answers.
key_big: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons.
body_html:
How to think about it

A force is a push or a pull. It is measured in newtons (N).

  • Contact forces: friction, normal force, tension, air resistance, upthrust. Non-contact forces: gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic.
  • A force can change an object's speed, direction, shape or size, cause a turning effect, or exert pressure.
  • Mass (kg) is the amount of matter; weight (N) is the pull of gravity on it.
  • Pressure = force ÷ area, in Pa (N/m²). A smaller area gives a greater pressure.
Example

A force of 60 N acts on 0.2 m². Pressure?

60 ÷ 0.2

Answer: 300 Pa

Example

Why does a knife cut better when sharp?

Smaller area

Answer: The same force gives a greater pressure.

Common mistakes

  • Calling gravity a contact force. It acts at a distance.
  • Thinking mass and weight are the same. Weight is a force in newtons.
  • Thinking a large area gives a large pressure. It is the opposite.
  • Saying a straw 'sucks' the drink. Atmospheric pressure pushes it up.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter (kg) and is the same everywhere. Weight is the gravitational force on the object (N) and changes with gravity.

faq.q: What are contact and non-contact forces?
faq.a: Contact forces act when objects touch (friction, tension). Non-contact forces act at a distance (gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic).

faq.q: What is the unit of pressure?
faq.a: The pascal (Pa), which is one newton per square metre (N/m²).

It keeps moving at the same speed in the same direction.
items.e: Balanced forces: no change in motion. Unbalanced forces: speeding up, slowing down or changing direction.

items.e: Contact forces act only when objects touch. Non-contact forces (gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic) act at a distance.

items.q: An astronaut goes from the Earth to the Moon. What happens?
c: Her mass and weight both decrease.
Her mass decreases but her weight stays the same.
Her mass stays the same but her weight decreases.
items.e: Gravity on the Moon is weaker.

items.q: What is pressure?
c: the force acting on each unit of area
items.e: pressure = force ÷ area.

items.q: What causes the pressure of a gas in a container?
c: Particles colliding with the walls of the container
items.e: More collisions, more pressure.

items.q: Why do snowshoes stop you sinking into snow?
c: They spread your weight over a large area, so the pressure is lower.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: A force of 500 N gives a pressure of 250 Pa. What is the area?
items.e: Area = force ÷ pressure = 500 ÷ 250 = 2 m².

items.q: Why do people wear snowshoes or use wide skis to walk on deep snow?
c: They spread the weight over a large area, so the pressure is lower.
items.e: Large area, low pressure.

items.q: A pressure of 15 Pa acts on an area of 4 m². What is the force?
items.e: Force = pressure × area = 15 × 4 = 60 N.

items.q: A force of 40 N acts on an area of 5 m². What is the pressure?
items.e: Pressure = force ÷ area = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 Pa (N/m²).

items.q: A brick is placed on a table first on its largest face, then on its smallest face. When is the pressure on the table greatest?
c: it is the same both ways
items.e: The weight is the same; a smaller area gives a greater pressure.

items.q: Why do caterpillar tracks help heavy tanks cross mud?
c: The tracks have a large area, so the pressure on the ground is low.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: Why does a drawing pin have a sharp point and a wide head?
c: Both ends give the same pressure.
The point gives a high pressure on the board; the head gives a low pressure on your thumb.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: A pressure of 1500 Pa acts on an area of 0.1 m². What is the force?
items.e: Force = pressure × area = 1500 × 0.1 = 150 N.

items.q: If the same force acts on a smaller area, what happens to the pressure?
items.e: Inverse relationship.

items.q: Why do tractors have wide tyres?
c: To spread the weight and reduce the pressure on soft ground.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: A pressure of 300 Pa acts on an area of 2 m². What is the force?
items.e: Force = pressure × area = 300 × 2 = 600 N.

items.q: A force of 200 N gives a pressure of 2000 Pa. What is the area?
items.e: Area = force ÷ pressure = 200 ÷ 2000 = 0.1 m².

items.q: A force of 40 N gives a pressure of 400 Pa. What is the area?
items.e: Area = force ÷ pressure = 40 ÷ 400 = 0.1 m².

items.q: What is the unit of pressure?
c: newtons per square metre (N/m²), also called pascals (Pa)
items.e: 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

items.q: A force of 20 N gives a pressure of 4 Pa. What is the area?
items.e: Area = force ÷ pressure = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 m².

items.q: Aisha wears high-heeled shoes and then flat shoes. Why do the high heels sink into soft grass more?
c: The force is smaller with high heels.
The same weight acts on a smaller area, so the pressure is greater.
Flat shoes have a smaller area.
items.e: Pressure = force ÷ area.

items.q: Why do high heels damage some floors more than flat shoes?
c: Pressure does not depend on area.
Flat shoes have a smaller area.
The small heel area gives a much larger pressure.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: A stool exerts a pressure of 200 N/m² on an area of 4 m². What is the force?
items.e: force = pressure × area = 200 × 4.

items.q: Earthquakes and tsunamis release huge forces. Why do engineers in some countries build earthquake-resistant buildings?
c: to reduce damage and save lives when these forces act on buildings
items.e: Understanding forces helps us design safer structures.

items.q: Why is it easier to push a nail into wood point first?
c: Wood is softer at the point.
The small area of the point gives a high pressure.
Force is bigger at the point.
items.e: Same force: smaller area → bigger pressure; bigger area → smaller pressure.

items.q: Which statement about gravitational force is correct?
c: It only acts when objects touch.
It is a non-contact force that pulls objects towards the Earth.
It pushes objects away from the Earth.
items.e: Gravity acts at a distance.

items.q: How do you drink through a straw?
c: The drink is lighter than air.
You lower the air pressure in the straw, and atmospheric pressure pushes the drink up.
The straw pulls the drink up.
items.e: There is no 'suction force'.

A gas is in a sealed container. What happens to its pressure if more gas is pumped in?
items.e: More particles hit the walls each second.

items.q: A car brakes and slows down. Which force mainly causes this?
c: friction between the brakes and the wheels, and the tyres and the road
items.e: Friction acts against motion.

items.q: How does a suction cup stick to a smooth wall?
c: Glue in the cup holds it.
Air is pushed out, so the air pressure outside pushes the cup against the wall.
items.e: Atmospheric pressure does the pushing.

items.q: Why can a submarine dive only to a certain depth?
c: There is no water deep down.
Water pressure increases with depth and could crush the hull.
items.e: Deep-sea submarines need very strong hulls.

items.q: A gas is in a sealed container. What happens to its pressure if some gas is let out?
items.e: Fewer particles hit the walls each second.

items.q: A pressure of 800 Pa acts on an area of 0.1 m². What is the force?
items.e: Force = pressure × area = 800 × 0.1 = 80 N.

items.q: Why are dams built thicker at the bottom than at the top?
c: Water pressure is greater at greater depth.
Water is lighter at the bottom.
items.e: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth.
